keyTakeaways: Hot partitions are the killer at scale — coalesce duplicate reads
ScyllaDB (C++) avoids JVM GC pauses that plagued Cassandra
A request-coalescing data service layer smooths spikes
Rust data services in front of the DB
summary: Discord outgrew Cassandra (GC pauses, hot partitions, maintenance pain) and migrated its trillions of messages to ScyllaDB, a C++ rewrite of Cassandra. They added intermediary "data services" in Rust to coalesce concurrent requests for the same data, taming hot partitions.
title: How Discord Stores Trillions of Messages

keyTakeaways: Choose a shard key that matches your access pattern
Bucket by channel + time for range scans
Cassandra for write-heavy, append-only data
Idempotency via monotonic Snowflake IDs
summary: The original story: Discord moved from MongoDB to Cassandra for messages, choosing a schema partitioned by (channel_id, time bucket) so a channel’s messages stay together and are efficiently range-scanned. A great primer on picking a shard key.
title: How Discord Stores Billions of Messages

keyTakeaways: Actor model (BEAM) for millions of stateful connections
A single hot process becomes the bottleneck — parallelize fan-out
Read-mostly global state needs special handling
summary: Discord’s realtime fan-out runs on Elixir/Erlang’s actor model. They hit limits when a huge guild caused a single process to fall behind, and fixed it with a "manifold" for parallel fan-out and Erlang’s fastglobal for hot read-mostly data.
title: How Discord Scaled Elixir to 5,000,000 Concurrent Users

keyTakeaways: Encode time + shard + sequence into a 64-bit ID
Time-sortable IDs avoid a central ID service
Logical shards mapped to physical DBs allow rebalancing
summary: Instagram needed globally-unique, roughly time-sortable IDs across a sharded Postgres fleet without a central coordinator. Their answer: 64-bit IDs built from a timestamp + shard id + per-shard sequence, generated inside Postgres with a stored procedure.
title: Sharding & IDs at Instagram

keyTakeaways: Append-only immutable cells simplify replication & auditing
Layer a KV abstraction over sharded MySQL
Trigger-based derived indexes and change feeds
summary: Uber built "Schemaless" — an append-only, sharded key-value store layered on top of many MySQL instances — to get horizontal write scale and operational simplicity while keeping MySQL’s reliability. Data is stored as immutable cells; buffered writes and triggers drive derived data.
title: Designing Schemaless, Uber’s Scalable Datastore Using MySQL

keyTakeaways: Postgres rewrites every index on any update (write amplification)
InnoDB’s clustered index + secondary indexes via primary key
Replication format matters at scale
summary: A famously controversial deep-dive: Uber hit Postgres pain points (write amplification from its index/tuple model, replication inefficiency, connection overhead) and moved to MySQL/InnoDB. A must-read on how storage-engine internals affect scale.
title: Why Uber Engineering Switched from Postgres to MySQL

keyTakeaways: Idempotency keys make retries safe
Stash the request + response so replays return the same result
Separate the idempotency layer from business logic
summary: Airbnb built idempotency into their payments layer so network retries never charge a guest twice. They use client-supplied idempotency keys, a stateful request-stashing store, and careful transaction boundaries to make retries safe.
title: Avoiding Double Payments in a Distributed Payments System

keyTakeaways: Erasure coding cuts storage cost vs full replication
Immutable content-addressed blocks
Building your own storage can beat cloud at massive scale
summary: Dropbox migrated off Amazon S3 to their own exabyte-scale storage system, Magic Pocket. Files are split into blocks, replicated and later erasure-coded across zones, with a sharded metadata layer tracking where each block lives.
title: Inside the Magic Pocket

keyTakeaways: Tail latency, not average, defines user experience
Deep observability: tcpdump → kernel counters → root cause
Edge/network internals (SYN cookies, backlog queues) matter
summary: A customer reported occasional latency spikes to Cloudflare’s edge. This post walks the full debugging journey — from tcpdump and packet captures down to the Linux kernel’s SYN-flood defenses and network stack — to find the culprit. A masterclass in diagnosing tail latency.
title: The story of one latency spike

keyTakeaways: V8 isolates are far lighter than containers
Hide startup latency behind the TLS handshake
Multi-tenancy via isolates, not VMs
summary: Cloudflare Workers use V8 isolates instead of containers/VMs, so code runs with effectively zero cold start. They even warm the isolate during the TLS handshake, hiding startup entirely behind the connection setup.
title: Eliminating cold starts with Cloudflare Workers

keyTakeaways: Active-active beats active-passive for failover
Cross-region async replication with eventual consistency
Regularly practice regional failover (chaos)
summary: Netflix runs the same stack active-active across AWS regions so an entire region can fail with users transparently served from another. Cassandra replicates data cross-region and Zuul routes traffic; they validate it by regularly evacuating a region.
title: Active-Active for Multi-Regional Resiliency

keyTakeaways: Replicate cache across AZs for resiliency + locality
Global cache warming and cross-region replication
Cache is a first-class tier, not an afterthought
summary: EVCache is Netflix’s distributed caching layer (built on Memcached) that replicates cached data across zones and regions for low-latency reads everywhere. It absorbs enormous read volume and shields backing stores.
title: Caching for a Global Netflix (EVCache)

keyTakeaways: Idempotency keys turn unsafe retries into safe ones
Persist request fingerprint + response
Exponential backoff with jitter for retries
summary: Stripe’s canonical explainer on idempotency keys: how clients can safely retry POST requests over an unreliable network without double-charging, using an idempotency layer that records and replays the first response.
title: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency

keyTakeaways: Dual-write to old + new, backfill, dual-read, then cut over
Never do a big-bang migration on live data
Verify old vs new continuously during migration
summary: How Stripe changes the schema of a table serving live traffic with zero downtime, using the classic four-step dual-write / backfill / dual-read / cutover pattern. The reference playbook for safe data migrations.
title: Online migrations at scale

keyTakeaways: Token bucket in Redis for distributed rate limiting
Load shedding: drop low-priority work first
Different limiters for different failure modes
summary: Stripe walks through the rate limiters and load shedders that protect their API — a token-bucket limiter in Redis plus request prioritization so critical traffic survives when the system is overloaded.
title: Scaling your API with rate limiters

keyTakeaways: A central authority can be simpler than pure CRDT/OT
Conflict resolution at property granularity (LWW)
In-memory doc state + change relay
summary: Figma’s realtime collaboration isn’t CRDTs or OT — it’s a simpler last-writer-wins model on a per-property basis, coordinated by a central server that holds the document in memory and relays changes to all clients.
title: How Figma’s multiplayer technology works

keyTakeaways: Vertical partitioning buys time before horizontal sharding
A routing/proxy layer hides sharding from the app
Colocate related data to avoid cross-shard queries
summary: Figma scaled a single Postgres to a partitioned, horizontally-sharded fleet. They describe vertical partitioning by table first, then horizontal sharding with a routing layer, all while keeping the application mostly unaware.
title: How Figma’s databases team lived to tell the scale

keyTakeaways: Push heavy shared state to an edge cache
Lazy-load per-client data instead of full sync
Edge caches reduce origin load and latency
summary: As Slack teams grew to hundreds of thousands of users, sending each client the full user/channel state got too expensive. Flannel is an edge cache that holds this data near clients and lazily serves only what each client needs.
title: Flannel: An Application-Level Edge Cache to Make Slack Scale

keyTakeaways: Put a durable log (Kafka) in front of a queue for burst absorption
Decouple enqueue rate from processing rate
Idempotent workers for at-least-once delivery
summary: Slack’s Redis-based async job queue buckled under load spikes. They re-architected it with Kafka as a durable buffer in front of Redis, decoupling enqueue from execution so bursts no longer overwhelmed the system.
title: Scaling Slack’s Job Queue

keyTakeaways: Multi-tenancy + self-service for many internal customers
Pluggable storage engines behind one API
Operability is a first-class design goal
summary: Twitter built Manhattan, a multi-tenant, eventually-consistent distributed key-value database, to replace a sprawl of Cassandra clusters. It emphasizes operability, pluggable storage engines, and self-service for internal teams.
title: Manhattan, our real-time, multi-tenant distributed database

keyTakeaways: Caching tiers absorb the read-heavy timeline load
Hybrid fan-out for the timeline (push + pull)
Custom hardware/data-center investment at scale
summary: A tour of Twitter’s infrastructure evolution — from a Ruby monolith to services, custom hardware, Manhattan, caching tiers, and the timeline fan-out — and the lessons of running one of the busiest realtime products.
title: The Infrastructure Behind Twitter: Scale

keyTakeaways: The append-only log is the unifying data primitive
Operating Kafka at trillions/day needs custom tuning
Replication = replaying a log; streams unify batch + realtime
summary: LinkedIn — the birthplace of Kafka — runs over 7 trillion messages/day across 100+ clusters. This post covers the custom patches and operational practices (their internal fork, tiered storage ideas, scaling brokers) that keep Kafka healthy at that volume. The append-only log as the backbone of a company’s data.
title: How LinkedIn customizes Apache Kafka for 7 trillion messages per day

keyTakeaways: Encode shard id inside every object id
No cross-shard joins — denormalize instead
Boring, well-understood tech scales predictably
summary: Pinterest deliberately chose "boring" manual sharding over fancy distributed databases: IDs encode the shard, there are no cross-shard joins, and all data is denormalized. A masterclass in trading flexibility for predictable scale.
title: Sharding Pinterest: How we scaled our MySQL fleet

keyTakeaways: Modular monolith: boundaries without network calls
Microservices aren’t the only answer to a big codebase
Enforce component isolation in-process
summary: Rather than break their Rails monolith into microservices, Shopify made it a "modular monolith" with enforced component boundaries — keeping deploy simplicity while regaining the modularity that microservices promise.
title: Deconstructing the Monolith: Designing for Developer Productivity

keyTakeaways: Partition by workspace so related blocks colocate
Many logical shards per physical DB eases future splits
Double-write + backfill + verify for the live cutover
summary: Notion sharded its single Postgres (holding every block of every workspace) into 480 logical shards across physical instances, partitioning by workspace id so a workspace’s data stays together. Covers the tricky live migration too.
title: Herding elephants: Lessons learned from sharding Postgres at Notion

keyTakeaways: One uniform "block" primitive for all content
Recursive parent/child references model any structure
Flexibility comes from a simple, general data model
summary: Everything in Notion — text, pages, databases — is a "block" with a type, properties, and a list of child block ids. This uniform recursive model is what lets users nest and transform content arbitrarily.
title: The data model behind Notion’s flexibility

keyTakeaways: Availability over consistency (AP) for the shopping cart
Consistent hashing spreads data + minimizes reshuffling
Quorums (W+R>N) tune the consistency/latency trade-off
summary: The paper that launched the NoSQL era: Amazon’s Dynamo trades strong consistency for always-on availability using consistent hashing, vector clocks, quorums, and hinted handoff. The intellectual ancestor of Cassandra and DynamoDB.
title: Amazon’s Dynamo (Werner Vogels / SOSP paper)
